lines.text: Give me a minute, I'm wedging this one and it'll go where I put it.
My back went two summers ago and I can still put a tree down exactly where I want it. Getting up off the ground after is the trouble, and my wife has heard that one often enough to say it for me.
Below the town the Barkhide eat the low growth back to the dirt. On ground like that a log walks down to the road one-handed.
There's not a stick left in there worth me walking in for, and I've not had a saw out past the east stair in four years.
No Barkhide on those slopes now, so the low growth has come right up and the young trees under it all came on in one season. The canopy is thinner than when we were cutting under it.
Grown Webvern silk I can tell through a glove. Both hands on a strand, pull as hard as I like, it holds. Young stuff comes apart on the frame while you're winding it.
Second grade. It doesn't leave here as anything else.
And the moths make none of it — that's Webvern work, all of it. The stall on the corner will tell you different and the stall has never had a hand on the stuff.
You want the winding house? It's the — no, wait, are you going up the east stair, because I'm not allowed on the east stair.

Gloomgrub are the little ones and they turn into the big ones out of the high lines, only they don't, they're a different thing altogether, and the silk comes off the wings when they come through and the lamps go out, whoomf.
One went down my collar and got away — hold on, that's my sister, she's not meant to be
Floor stair, was it? They all come up that way. On the walk we would have called that a floor matter, and on the floor they would have sent it up to the walk.
In my day a person knew which.

That was the lampkeeper's family who sent it up, his father before him and his father's brother as well. I came up to the walk myself the year they re-cut the lower stair, which was the year after my father died, or the year before it — I have had it both ways round for a while now.
First the lower run. Forty-one, forty-two, forty — no. Lost my place. Start again.
Oil's in the shed behind the winding house. — Was it oil you wanted?
Pell has the stair. Mine's the walk, and mine is two hundred and eleven. In the autumn the moths put the lot out. Then it is two hundred and eleven again, from the first lamp up.
We cut marked stands and nothing else. The marks come down from the town.
Webvern in the tops over this stand, so we cut round those trees. Reason given is the silk pays better than the timber. Off the stand by dusk, and the reason given there is Duskstalk.
Two hours out at the start and two hours back at the end, and that is in the terms.
